analysis.one_liner: Removes Medicare's exclusion so it covers hearing aids and related exams.
analysis.headline: The bill to add hearing aid coverage to Medicare has sat without committee action since January 2025, despite 32 cosponsors from both parties.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare currently refuses to pay for hearing aids or the exams to fit them, by law. This bill would strike that exclusion starting in 2026, so millions of older adults with hearing loss could get hearing aids covered like glasses-style benefits in other programs. It also orders a government study of which programs help people get hearing aids and how well they work. It was introduced with bipartisan cosponsors and referred to two House committees, where it has not moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries with hearing loss. Hearing aids typically cost thousands of dollars per pair and are excluded from Medicare, so most seniors pay out of pocket or go without. Untreated hearing loss is linked to social isolation and cognitive decline, so coverage would help seniors both financially and health-wise. The bill takes effect for items and services furnished on or after January 1, 2026.

how_it_helps.text: The bill deletes the statutory exclusion at Social Security Act section 1862(a)(7) that bars Medicare from paying for hearing aids or examinations for them, making hearing aids a covered item under Medicare [S3].
Coverage would apply to items and services furnished on or after January 1, 2026 [S3].

The Government Accountability Office must study federal programs and health insurance coverage that help people with hearing loss get hearing aids, and report to Congress within 18 months with recommendations [S3].
The Congressional Research Service describes the bill simply as allowing Medicare coverage of hearing aids and related examinations [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If the bill passed, the federal government (and Medicare premiums) would pay for hearing aids and related exams for beneficiaries, a new mandatory spending obligation. The bill text does not specify offsets or financing, so the cost would fall on taxpayers and Medicare generally rather than on a named industry.

drawbacks.text: Adding hearing aid coverage is new federal spending on top of Medicare's existing financing shortfalls, and the bill contains no financing mechanism or offset — the cost lands on taxpayers and Medicare's budget [S3].

The bill does not set a benefit design, copay structure, or dispensing rules; it simply removes the exclusion, leaving the details — and the costs — to be worked out through Medicare's normal processes [S3].

Since 2022, over-the-counter hearing aids have been available without a prescription for mild-to-moderate loss, so critics can argue that a full coverage mandate is more than some beneficiaries need; the bill still helps those with severe loss, who need prescription-fit devices and exams.
Supporters acknowledge the fiscal cost: a hearing aid benefit would be one of the larger additions to Medicare's benefit package in years, which is the standard reason such bills stall in committee.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: hearing aids are one of the largest out-of-pocket health costs seniors face, and Medicare's exclusion is a 1965-era artifact. The cost is genuine new federal spending with no offset in the bill, which is a fair objection in a period of Medicare financing pressure. A well-designed version could set copays or coordinate with the over-the-counter market for mild loss; this bill leaves those details open. On balance it is a straightforward pro-senior benefit whose main obstacle is cost, not design.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees in January 2025, and neither committee has taken it up since.

narrative.text: Representative Debbie Dingell introduced the Medicare Hearing Aid Coverage Act on January 16, 2025, with an initial bipartisan group including Representative Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania [S3].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee for consideration of provisions in their jurisdictions [S5].
The bill has 32 cosponsors, 30 Democrats and 2 Republicans [S4].
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the action history through the end of the record [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed: seniors still pay full price for hearing aids, and Medicare and the federal budget avoid the new spending the bill would create. Hearing aid retailers and manufacturers keep selling at full price, unaffected.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: seniors pay, Medicare saves

for.name: Rep. Debbie Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to remove Medicare's hearing aid exclusion and assembled bipartisan original cosponsors [S3].

for.name: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor, one of two Republicans among the 32 cosponsors [S4].

for.what_they_did: Signed on in support, giving the bill 32 total cosponsors [S4].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Referred committee (chair has not scheduled action)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 16, 2025; no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill appears in the record since [S5].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Referred committee (has jurisdiction over Medicare financing; chair has not scheduled action)
against.what_they_did: Received a concurrent referral on January 16, 2025; the committee, which controls Medicare benefit changes, has taken no recorded action on the bill [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Support is heavily Democratic (30 of 32 cosponsors) but includes 2 Republicans, and there is no recorded opposition — the bill has simply not been scheduled for any committee action.

industries.note: Medicare coverage would create a large new paying customer base for hearing aid makers and audiologists, whose devices Medicare would pay full freight for. Their interest here runs alongside seniors': the industry gains volume while seniors gain access, though coverage without price negotiation also lets the industry bill Medicare's open-ended rates.

industries.industry: Medicare beneficiaries with untreated hearing loss
industries.note: Not an industry, but the core constituency: seniors who currently pay thousands of dollars out of pocket would have hearing aids and fitting exams covered starting January 2026.
New mandatory Medicare spending with no offset in the bill; taxpayers and Medicare trust funds absorb the cost.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits with two committees and has no scheduled hearing or markup. Medicare benefit expansions of this size usually need a chair's decision and often move only as part of a larger package or via a different vehicle; with 32 cosponsors and no committee action more than a year in, the likeliest path is that it dies quietly at the end of the 119th Congress unless sponsors fold its language into a broader Medicare package or it is reintroduced.
